body: PHIL 1 let out at a quarter to eleven, and Jack has been horizontal ever since, paying down Wednesday. Theo is out. The noon light lies across 412 in a long bright bar from the window to the closet door, and the Augustine is tented open on Jack’s chest at Book Four with the Housman inside it, a war in the middle of a conversion. The RAZR goes against his ribs, and two minutes later it goes again.

body.text: Lunch @ Anacapa 12:30? Saving you a seat. Bring jokes. -K
COSTIGAN. TIDE OFFICE, UCEN. 12:30. I NEED A CATHOLIC FOR TEN MINUTES. —M

body: He never did save her number. He looks at both screens with the phone held at the angle where it lights. One of them is holding a chair for him. The other has apparently run out of Catholics.

Anacapa Commons at half past twelve is a thousand freshmen and one waffle iron. The waffle line goes back past the cereal dispensers; the panini line goes out the door into the sun. Kevin has the corner table by the window, as promised, his tray squared to the edge of it and on the tray a salad that is less a salad than a set of figures: grilled chicken, egg whites, chickpeas, one measured fist of spinach. He’s back in a quarter-zip, Bellarmine maroon, zipped to the collarbone.
Jack sits down with a square of Thursday lasagna and two cookies, grinning before he’s all the way in the chair. He has been grinning about it, on and off, for a day and a half.
“So,” he says. “You and Margot.”

Kevin’s fork stops on its way up, a cube of chicken on the end of it. Behind him somebody drops a tray, and the near half of the Commons applauds, and the fork waits through all of it. Then the big laugh comes, the team-captain laugh that fills a table, and the chicken goes where it was going.
“Margot and me,” Kevin says. “Sure. Let’s go with that.” He points the empty fork across the table. “Respectfully, bro, she’d dissect me. For science.”

response: “So could I,” Kevin says, and grins, and moves the chickpeas over to make room for a new subject. He’s seen the wall post — all of Delgado has seen the wall post, both exclamation points — and he wants to know where she’s taking him Friday. “She won’t say.” “That tracks. She ran the cleanup like a cattle drive.” Does Jack own anything warm? Kevin listens to every answer with his chin on his fist, sunny and interested, as if Friday were the only news on the board.

Kevin’s laugh lands right on cue. “Tell Theo,” he says, “and I tell Becca you can’t tell a heifer from a steer.” “I can tell a heifer from a steer.” “Can you, though? On a Friday night? With the lights off?” He takes one of Jack’s cookies as a fine, and Jack lets him have it.

Jack lets it go and asks about the quiz instead, and Kevin gives him three minutes on chirality with the salt and pepper shakers: two molecules built of the same parts, mirror images, that won’t lie down on top of each other however you turn them. Jack follows it as far as the pepper. B-plus, Kevin says. Again. Gregory the green highlighter came through. At the tray return, sliding his tray onto the belt, Kevin says, “Thanks, man,” and is gone toward the Chem building at a jog before Jack can work out what for.

s09b.slug: THURSDAY · 12:30 PM · THE UCEN, THE TIDE NEWSROOM
body: The *Marisol Tide* lives up a flight of stairs from the Panda Express, in a long room that smells of orange chicken and toner and has never been aired out. Back issues stand along the walls in twine-tied bundles, a geological history of student outrage. On the desk by the window a dead iMac G4 — the white dome, the lamp-arm neck — has been put to work holding up the AP Stylebook, and beside it a living one hums under Margot’s hands. She is the only person in the room. “Sit,” she says, typing. “Ten minutes. I meant it.”

body.text: His flannel is on top of the dead iMac, folded in a square as tight as a flag at a Youngstown funeral. “It’s been washed,” Margot says. “Don’t read into it.”

body: On the screen, under MEMO — EDITORIAL BOARD — RE: COVERAGE, is a pitch. “There’s no faith page,” Margot says. “There will be. The board thinks religion here is a lifestyle section. I need one quote from an actual believer so they can’t say I made you up.” She turns the chair to face him. “What does your Church do that’s a story and not a scandal?”

The cursor blinks while he thinks. “Somebody sits with the dying,” he says. “Every parish. Every night of the week, somebody’s in a hospital chair next to somebody nobody else is coming to see. Nobody’s ever written it up. It hasn’t got a villain.”
Margot turns back and types it, all of it, in his order, without comment, and hits save.

body.text: “The pie was adequate,” she says.
“The pecan was adequate,” she says. “Lena ate three pieces.”
“Rhubarb is a vegetable,” she says. “I looked it up. I’m told that’s the point.”

body: “You and Kevin,” Jack says, and does the eyebrows.
Margot regards him for some time. “Costigan,” she says, “your powers of observation are exactly as advertised.” Then she’s back in the memo.
By her elbow is a paper coffee cup from the cart downstairs, and on the cardboard sleeve, in capitals he’d know anywhere — the RELIQUARY capitals — somebody has written BLACK. NO SUGAR. NO ARGUMENT.

“Lena came by at nine,” Margot says. She takes off the black frames and cleans them on her sweater, which they don’t need. “With two coffees. She didn’t say anything. She put that one down and left with the other one.” The glasses go back on. “I don’t know what to do with being *liked* by someone who thinks my mother was wrong.”

choices.text: “She doesn’t think your mother was wrong about loving him.”
response: Margot turns to the screen and types a whole sentence, fast, too fast for him to read from where he sits. Then she holds down the delete key and takes it back a letter at a time until the cursor is blinking at the start of an empty line. She drops the coffee cup in the recycling bin by the door without getting up, a clean shot. “Ten minutes,” she says. “Get out.”

choices.text: “Neither do I. Know what to do.”
response: Margot looks at him over the top of the monitor. “Good,” she says. “Then neither of us is lying.” She drinks what’s left of the coffee, which has been cold since ten, and makes a face at it, and finishes it, and drops the cup in the recycling bin by the door.

choices.text: “Drink the coffee. That’s what it’s for.”
response: “Coward,” Margot says — fondly, for Margot; the room warms by about a degree — and she picks up the cup and drinks the coffee, which has been cold since ten, all of it, looking at him over the lid. Then she drops the cup in the recycling bin by the door without turning around, a clean shot, and goes back to the memo.

body.text: *Margot and me. Sure.* Jack is still grinning about it at four o’clock, taking the basement stairs of Hollis two at a time.

On his way out of the *Tide* he passed the recycling bin by the door, and on top of the newsprint was the coffee cup, crushed flat, the sleeve still on it: BLACK. NO SUGAR. NO ARGUMENT. He’s still seeing it at four o’clock, taking the basement stairs of Hollis two at a time.

body: Hollis 108, the basement room with the one window at ankle height, sandals and bike tires going past in it. Evan Marsh at the front, grayer at the temples than in August, the bike clip still around one jean cuff, *Works of Love* open in front of him and bristling with Post-its.

body.text: Jack drops into the desk across the aisle from Lena. “It’s Thursday,” he says. She caps her pen and looks at him. “Then I’m okay,” she says, as if it had been written in her planner for a week, and uncaps it.

body: “Kierkegaard divides love in two,” Evan says. He never writes on the board. “Preferential love — the beloved, the friend, the ones you choose. And love of the neighbor, which you don’t get to choose, because the neighbor is whoever’s there.” He turns a page. “Kierkegaard thought the beloved and the friend were the self loved twice. Only the neighbor is the other.”
Lena’s pen comes up. “Then he never had a friend.”

Evan considers that. “He was engaged once,” he says. “Regine Olsen. He gave back the ring and wrote about her for the rest of his life.” He takes off his wire glasses, rubs the two red marks they’ve worn into the bridge of his nose, and puts them back on.

body.text: It is the second dead man’s marriage to walk into a philosophy class in two days. This time Jack keeps his mouth shut about it.

body: At ten to five Evan lets them go. Jack passes her paper across the aisle — “That They Can’t,” his red all through it from Wednesday night. She turns to page two first. She always does. His own paper doesn’t come back the other way.
“I’m not done with yours,” she says.
“When?”
“Sunday.”

response: At the bottom of page two, beside her best paragraph, in his red: *Cite me.* Her own margin word, in his handwriting. She makes a face like a stolen car that has come home washed and waxed, with a full tank.

choices.text: *You don’t believe a word of this.*
response: At the bottom of page two, in his red: *You don’t believe a word of this.* Her own line from last Thursday, returned in his hand to her page. She uncaps her pen and underlines it once, in her ink, under his. Then she caps the pen with a click you could hear in the hall.

At the bottom of page two, in his red: *Best thing you’ve written. It’s wrong.* She reads it. Then she folds the paper once, carefully, along the line of the staple, and slips it inside the cover of her Kierkegaard.

journal.title: Evan Marsh (TA)
journal.text: Thursday section, Hollis 108. Kierkegaard. Kind to the scared ones, murder on the lazy ones. Smokes American Spirits. Rides a bike. Came back from PERSONAL grayer. Told us we’d left out a driver. Says Kierkegaard was engaged once, gave back the ring, and wrote about her for the rest of his life.

s10.slug: FRIDAY · 5:59 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL
body: At a minute to six on Friday the Fishbowl is full of people who just happen to be there. Laney is on the long couch in her Pi Lam letters, pink on white, her feet tucked under her, doing nothing with tremendous concentration. Lena is on the arm of the same couch with a Hansen and Quinn open on her knee, because Laney dragged her down for what Laney called a study break, and she has been on the same page of the aorist since she sat. Theo is at the broken foosball table with the MacBook balanced across the goalie rods, editing something with the sound off. Kevin and Doug Pruitt have the far couch under the TV, where the President is at a podium in Pittsburgh talking about a secret plant in Iran, and Doug wants to know if Qom is near Bakersfield, because it sounds near Bakersfield.

Jack comes down in the Carhartt jacket, too big in the shoulders, because the wall post said to dress warm. At 5:59 a red pickup with Idaho plates turns into the circle out front and stops square in the fire lane, and Becca Lindell comes through both sets of doors at a ranch walk: Ropers, Wranglers, the Carhartt vest, the braid down her back as thick as a bell rope, the keys swinging off the steel carabiner on one finger. “I’m early,” she says, to everybody. “I’m always early. It’s a ranch thing.”
“Is she Amish,” Laney says, at a volume built for pageant stages, “or just punctual?”
Lena closes the grammar on one finger. “Laney. Be nice.” She means it. It’s in the finger, holding her place.
“I *am* nice,” says Laney. “I’m being *accurate*.”

Theo has already risen from the foosball table and crossed the room with his hand out, as if he’s been waiting his whole life to be introduced. “Becca. Theo Vance.” The handshake is perfect: warm, brief, a little reverent. “I’ve heard you can butcher a deer.”
Becca lights up like he’s asked after her family. “Elk too.”

Theo receives this as if handed a Fabergé egg, and goes back to the foosball table, and his thumbs go to work on the iPhone below the edge of it. Across the room, on the couch cushion, Laney’s pink BlackBerry buzzes. She reads it. She looks at Theo. Theo looks at the foosball men on their rods, at the middle distance, at nothing.
Kevin doesn’t look away from the TV. “Leave it alone,” he says.
“Leave what alone?” says Theo.
Nobody says.
Lena, from the arm of the couch, to Becca, kindly, meaning every word of it: “Have fun. He’ll try to explain football to you. Let him.”
“I’ll let him,” Becca says, and beams at her, and at Jack, and at the whole Fishbowl, which she seems to find lovely.

response: Laney blows him a kiss off the flat of her palm, full pageant. “*Never*, fireman.” The BlackBerry is buzzing again before the kiss has crossed the room.

Becca holds the Fishbowl door for him, and they go out across the lobby, and behind them the whole Fishbowl turns on its couches to watch through the glass — Laney, Theo, Kevin, Doug, the President of the United States — as if the lobby had come on TV.

Lena opens the grammar again to the page her finger was keeping. “I never do, Costigan.” She turns the page. Her composure is flawless. On the couch below her, Laney’s eyebrows have gone up into the copper hair and taken up residence.

s10b.slug: FRIDAY · 7:05 PM · MARISOL HIGH SCHOOL, MARINER FIELD
body: The Ranger is a ’94, red where it isn’t primer, with a feed-store sticker from Rathdrum on the back glass, and inside it smells like hay and old coffee and every pickup in Youngstown. Clipped to the driver’s visor is a St. Isidore the Farmer medal, the saint walking behind his plow. Becca drives with one hand at twelve o’clock and the other out the window, down Mission and up the hill, talking about Eli’s clutch like it’s a family member with a temper.

At the card table by the gate it’s five dollars a head, and Jack has his wallet out and Becca has already paid. “I asked, I pay,” she says. “Next time you can.” She buys the hot dogs too, and two cans of pop, and takes a stadium blanket out of the truck bed, red plaid, smelling of truck bed.

Mariner Field is every high-school field in America, which is the whole pleasure of it: the lights coming on against a sky still pink over the hills, a band in wool coats too hot for September, cut grass and kettle corn. The Marisol High Mariners against the Arroyo Seco Broncs, who came over the hills on two yellow buses and yell like four. Becca knows downs. She knows them the way Frank knows them, from the inside, and by the end of the first quarter she has explained a zone blitz to the grandfather in front of them and stood up twice to tell the referee about a hold he didn’t call.

Late in the second quarter the Mariners line up on fourth and one at the Broncs’ thirty-eight. Becca puts her hot dog down on the blanket, shuts her eyes, and says the Glory Be out loud, fast, all of it in the time it takes the quarterback to get under center — *as it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be* — and the quarterback sneaks it, and the pile leans, and the chains come out, and it’s a first down by the width of a hand. She opens her eyes. “See?” she says. “You can get through it while a cow’s kicking you.”

The Mariners’ mascot is a man in a sea captain’s coat and a foam peg leg who stumps up and down the track in front of the student section with a harpoon made of a pool noodle, and the student section calls him Ahab and chants it every time the Broncs have the ball. And Jack has the joke already built — the leg, the whale, which of the two teams is the whale, the whole timing of it down to the pause before the last line — and it’s built for someone who isn’t on these bleachers. He holds it. Then he puts it away, and eats his hot dog.

At halftime the PA comes on with Miley Cyrus, and the whole student section gets up on the benches to sing it, and so does Becca, who knows every word and doesn’t care in the slightest who sees her know them. She sits down pink and pleased. “I have two sisters,” she says, which explains it.
Then she turns to him on the blanket. “Teach me one of the proofs. The first one. The ones with numbers.” “The Five Ways.” “The first one.”

So he teaches her the First Way, on the home bleachers at Mariner Field, with mustard on his thumb. Things move — not just across a floor; they change, they go from could-be to is. A cold pan gets hot. But nothing gets itself from could-be to is; something already hot has to heat it. Line them up, the pan, the burner, the gas, and you can’t go back forever, because with no first there’s no second and no hot pan, and there’s the pan, hot. So there’s a first mover that nothing moved. “And this everyone understands to be God,” he says. “That’s Aquinas. That’s the end of it.”

Becca says it back perfectly. She does it with a newborn calf in a cold barn, a heat lamp, a generator, a diesel truck and her father, and doesn’t drop a step, and lands on *God* with both feet. “That’s good,” she says. “That’s *so* good.” She hugs her knees inside the blanket and looks at the empty field, happy, and the proof runs off her like rain off a Carhartt. Nothing soaks through.

“Do you ever think it might not be true?” she asks, as easily as asking whether he takes cream. Then, before he can answer: “I don’t. I’ve never once.” She turns and looks at him, honestly puzzled, the braid over one shoulder, sunburn along her part under the stadium lights. “Do you?”

choices.key: On the bleachers Becca asked if you ever think it might not be true. You said sometimes, at two in the morning.
response: She thinks about that with her whole face — eyebrows, mouth, freckles — as if it were a calf turned wrong. Then it clears. “Then I’ll pray for two in the morning,” she says, and picks her hot dog back up, and he believes her: every night, on the rosary, in Portolá Hall, with the lights out.

“Good,” Becca says. She means it entirely, all the way down, and pats his knee through the blanket: settled. The band comes back up the stairs. The teams come out of the field house. The third quarter starts as though nobody asked anything.

Becca laughs, a big ranch-kitchen laugh that turns the grandfather around in his seat. Then she folds her hands on the blanket, very serious, and adds the Cleveland Browns to her prayer list out loud, between Eli’s clutch and her mother’s bad knee.

s10c.slug: FRIDAY · 9:40 PM · PORTOLÁ HALL, THE PARKING LOT
body: The Mariners won it by a field goal with a minute to go, and Becca honked the Ranger’s horn twice at every light on Mission, for the team. Now the truck sits under the sodium light in the Portolá lot with the engine ticking as it cools. The cab has gone quiet. St. Isidore turns a little on his clip. Becca has the keys in her lap on the carabiner, and across the lot, through the eucalyptus, Delgado is lit up in its grid.

“That was a good game,” she says. He agrees, and it was. Then she leans across the bench seat, quick and certain, and kisses him on the cheek, high up, where the stubble starts, and sits back behind the wheel.
“So there’s no confusion,” she says.

response: She nods once, satisfied, like a gate latched. “Good night, Jack.” She goes up the walk to Portolá swinging the keys, and at the door she turns and waves with her whole arm, the pasture wave, until he waves back.

choices.key: In the Portolá lot you kissed Becca’s cheek back.
response: He leans across and kisses her cheek back. Sunburn and hay and Ivory soap. She laughs, pleased, gone pink all the way to the braid. “Okay then,” she says, and gets out of the truck still laughing.

She waits, the keys quiet in her lap. He doesn’t have the rest of it. She waits some more, kindly, with all the time in the world, and then she smiles at him under the sodium light. “Next Friday?” she says. “You can think about it.”

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion.

s10d.slug: FRIDAY · 10:02 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE LOBBY
body: Marcus is asleep at the front desk with his cheek on his orgo book. Laney Price is sitting on the desk beside him with her ankles crossed, swinging a Tory Burch flat off one toe, the pink BlackBerry held in both hands like a hymnal.
“Debrief, fireman.”

She wants it all. Is there a dowry, and is it cattle, and how many head. Did Idaho drive with one hand or two, because one hand is a *sign*. Her thumbs keep going on the BlackBerry the whole time, reporting to somebody mid-sentence.
“What’d y’all talk about?”

body.text: “God.” Laney lowers the phone an inch. “On a *second date*. Bless her heart, she’s going for the throat.”
“Football.” “Liar. Nobody talks about football at football.”
“The Browns.” “Precious, that’s not a topic. That’s a condolence.”
She leans in and squints at the side of his face, under the lobby fluorescents. “You’ve got Idaho on your face, sugar.”

body: Then, all innocence, the BlackBerry gone dark in her lap: “Lena’s on the east stairs. With *Wes*. Second floor.” She examines a nail. “I had to step over her, sugar. She waved me by like a crossing guard.” He’s already looking at the stairwell door. “In case you were wondering,” says Laney. “Which you weren’t.”

response: He takes the elevator. It comes down slow and goes up slow, past two, past three, and lets him out on four, and 412 is dark except for the blue of Theo’s MacBook. Theo is asleep with his headphones on and one hand still on the trackpad.

The east stairwell carries everything, and he hears her before he sees her: a long low laugh coming down the concrete. Lena is on the landing between two and three, on the step with her back to the wall and the LG at her ear, laughing at something a long way off. She sees him coming up and covers the phone with her palm.
“Was it a date?”
“It was football *and* a date.”

“Efficient,” Lena says. She’s back in New Orleans before he’s reached her step. He goes up past her on the rail side, and the laugh follows him a floor and a half, until the fire door on four shuts it off.

body: Sunday, and the light is all over 412 again, on the carpet and the milk crate and the Augustine on the desk. Jack is sitting on the edge of his bed in a T-shirt and yesterday’s dish-pit hands, working out which Mass, when the RAZR goes, and goes again a minute later.

body.text: Sully’s. Ten. Black and gold or don’t come. Dale’s saving the booth. —L.
9:30 Mass then Coffee & Donuts? I’m on hospitality. I’ll save you a maple bar :)

body: He owns one black T-shirt, which he is wearing, and nothing gold at all.

choices.key: Sunday you watched the Saints with Lena at Sully’s.
Sunday you went to the 9:30 with Becca and stayed for Coffee & Donuts.

body: Kevin drove, in a 49ers cap he says is a matter of conscience. Lena is in a black WHO DAT shirt with a gold ribbon through her hair, and at Sully’s she slides into the booth under the big screen, takes one look at Jack’s black T-shirt, digs in her tote, and lobs a string of gold Mardi Gras beads across the table at him. “There,” she says. “Now you’re dressed.” At the end of the bar Dale Wisniewski, in the Barry Sanders jersey, turns on his stool and lifts his coffee an inch. “The loud one.”

It’s an ugly game, gray and grinding up in Buffalo. Brees can’t find anybody, and in the fourth quarter Dale reads his line off the crawl and shakes his head at it — sixteen of twenty-nine, a hundred seventy-two yards, no touchdowns. Lena could not care less. She’s in love with the defense. Every time a Bills receiver goes down short of the sticks she’s on her feet, and every time Pierre Thomas lowers his head and runs into the middle of Buffalo she shouts, “Go to *work*, baby,” and Kevin pulls the 49ers cap down over his eyes. “This is so ugly,” she says, radiant. “I love it so much.”

On the tube TV in the corner the Browns are in Baltimore, and it’s worse than ugly. By the fourth quarter it’s thirty-four to three. “Three points,” Jack says. “*Three*.” Dale, who sat through oh-and-sixteen, looks over at the corner TV and back at Jack and gives him one slow nod, Warren to Youngstown.
At 10:41 the RAZR goes on the table.

body.text: Missed you! Saved you a maple bar anyway :)

body: Lena sees the screen as he tips it to the light. “Then go eat it, dish man,” she says, generous and exact, and turns back to the game. He doesn’t go. There’s a game on.

Twenty-seven to seven. On the last whistle Lena is out of the booth and up on the rail before the owner can get there, and she rings Sully’s brass bell herself, with her whole shoulder, till the Packers table applauds. In the Anacapa lot after, she wipes the 2–0 off the Odyssey’s back glass with one of Kevin’s gym socks from the back seat, over Kevin’s objections, and writes it big in the white La Vang polish: 3–0.

At nine, the college Mass: candles, three guitars, the hull going up into the dark. Numbers: Eldad and Medad prophesying in the camp without anybody’s permission, and Joshua wanting them stopped, and Moses: *Would that all the people of the Lord were prophets!* James, on the wages withheld from the workers, crying out. Then Mark, and the hard part. *If your hand causes you to sin, cut it off.*

Osei preaches from the step with the reading glasses on their cord. “Eldad and Medad were not on the list,” he says. “The Spirit does not check the guest list.” He takes the glasses off. “People hear the knife. I was a doctor; I hear the hand. It is yours. It does what you tell it. That is the frightening part.” He sits.
Jack’s right hand is on his knee. He leaves it there.

At the sign of peace he turns, and in the last pew, in black, with a reporter’s notebook closed on her knee, is Margot Lindqvist. “For the *Tide*,” she says, before he can ask. By Communion the last pew is empty.

The 9:30 is babies and the people who were up with them, sunburned fathers, a row of Vietnamese grandmothers in cardigans, the blue glass bright with morning. Gus Ferreira takes the opening hymn at the organ like a tuna boat taking a swell. Becca is beside Jack in a clean Carhartt vest over a church blouse, a rosary wound twice around her wrist, singing all four verses without the book.

Numbers: Eldad and Medad prophesying in the camp without anybody’s permission, and Joshua wanting them stopped, and Moses: *Would that all the people of the Lord were prophets!* James, on the wages withheld from the workers, crying out. Then Mark, and the hard part. *If your hand causes you to sin, cut it off.*

Osei preaches from the step with the reading glasses on their cord. “Eldad and Medad were not on the list,” he says. “The Spirit does not check the guest list.” He takes the glasses off. “People hear the knife. I was a doctor; I hear the hand. It is yours. It does what you tell it. That is the frightening part.” He sits.
Jack’s right hand is on his knee. He leaves it there.

Afterward the courtyard fills up around the folding tables under the olive tree, and the sprinkler hisses at the hedge. Becca is behind Coffee & Donuts in a hospitality apron with ST. BRENDAN’S ironed onto it, and she knows everybody’s order before they reach the front: decaf for the old man with the cane, two sugars for the grandmother in the lavender cardigan, one glazed cut in half for twins who can’t be trusted with a whole. Mrs. Fitch takes her coffee to a folding chair and watches the two of them over the rim.

Tyler Brandt finds Jack by the urns and fist-bumps him without asking. “Brother. You stood me up Wednesday.” “I was asleep.” “I prayed harder.” Tyler nods across at the table — the braid, the apron, the line moving like a clock — and lowers his voice to something like reverence. “Becca Lindell, brother. That’s a woman with a plan.”

By eleven Mrs. Fitch has said “you two” twice, and one of the Coffee & Donuts ladies has said it once, in the tone of settled business. The maple bar is waiting for him on a napkin with JACK on it in marker, in Becca’s poster lettering. “I said I would,” Becca says, and hands it over, and watches him take the first bite.

body.text: 3–0. Ugly and beautiful. Tell Becca hi. —L.

body: That night, cutting across the Anacapa lot on the way back from the library, he passes the Odyssey under its lamp. 3–0, big and white on the back glass. She wrote it anyway.

Theo is asleep on top of his comforter with the MacBook open beside him, and on the screen, paused, is the wake: a crooked frame, shot from somewhere around his hip, of the Mason jar and the lawn chair and Laney in the black peacoat, her face crumpled, mouth open, mid-sob, her hands a few inches apart. The screen saver hasn’t found it yet. It’s most of the light in the room.

body.text: There’s still a smear of white polish on the heel of Jack’s hand from holding the bottle in the Anacapa lot.
body.else: On the desk is a napkin that says JACK in marker, with nothing left on it but sugar.

body: At 11:41 something whispers under the door — paper, sliding on carpet. No knock. By the time he has it in his hand, the hall outside is quiet both ways.
It’s his paper. “That a Man and a Woman Can Be Friends,” two pages, stapled, and her red all through it.

body.text: In the first margin her *Cite me.* is underlined twice: his stolen word, stolen back.

body.title: That a Man and a Woman Can Be Friends — J. Costigan (red: M.B.)
body.text:
